claim: Newborns are unable to reach the adult-level humoral immune response partly due to the potent immunoregulatory role of IL-10.
source: Newborns are unable to reach the adult-level humoral immune response partly due to the potent immunoregulatory role of IL-10.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that draws on established scientific knowledge about neonatal immunity and IL-10's role.

claim: Increased IL-10 production by neonatal B cells has been attributed to the larger population of IL-10-producing CD43+ B-1 cells in neonates.
source: Increased IL-10 production by neonatal B cells has been attributed to the larger population of IL-10-producting CD43+ B-1 cells in neonates.
evidence: This statement references prior research findings about neonatal B cell populations.

claim: Neonatal mouse CD43- non-B-1 cells produce substantial amounts of IL-10 following B cell antigen receptor (BCR) activation.
source: Here, we show that neonatal mouse CD43- non-B-1 cells also produce substantial amounts of IL-10 following B cell antigen receptor (BCR) activation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: In neonatal mouse CD43- non-B-1 cells, BCR engagement activated STAT5 under the control of phosphorylated forms of signaling molecules Syk, Btk, PKC, FAK, and Rac1.
source: In neonatal mouse CD43- non-B-1 cells, BCR engagement activated STAT5 under the control of phosphorylated forms of signaling molecules Syk, Btk, PKC, FAK, and Rac1.
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2, 3, and 6.

claim: Neonatal STAT5 activation led to IL-6 production.
source: Neonatal STAT5 activation led to IL-6 production, which in turn was responsible for IL-10 production in an autocrine/paracrine fashion through the activation of STAT3.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: IL-6 produced by neonatal STAT5 activation was responsible for IL-10 production in an autocrine/paracrine fashion through the activation of STAT3.
source: Neonatal STAT5 activation led to IL-6 production, which in turn was responsible for IL-10 production in an autocrine/paracrine fashion through the activation of STAT3.
evidence: This mechanism is demonstrated through experimental data in Figures 3, 4, and 5.

claim: Elevated expression of IL-6Rα in neonatal B cells rendered them highly susceptible to IL-6-mediated STAT3 phosphorylation and IL-10 production.
source: In addition to the increased IL-6 production in response to BCR stimulation, elevated expression of IL-6Rα expression in neonatal B cells rendered them highly susceptible to IL-6-mediated STAT3 phosphorylation and IL-10 production.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: IL-10 secreted from neonatal mouse CD43- non-B-1 cells was sufficient to inhibit TNF-α secretion by macrophages.
source: Finally, IL-10 secreted from neonatal mouse CD43- non-B-1 cells was sufficient to inhibit TNF-α secretion by macrophages.
evidence: This functional consequence is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 7.

claim: Infants and neonates demonstrate high susceptibility to infection, leading to 40% of the annual death of approximately 7 million children under the age of 5 years worldwide.
source: Infants and neonates demonstrate high susceptibility to infection, leading to 40% of the annual death of approximately 7 million children under the age of 5 years worldwide (Bhutta and Black, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Bhutta and Black, 2013.

claim: Fetomaternal immune tolerance is essential to suppress rejection during pregnancy.
source: Fetomaternal immune tolerance is essential to suppress rejection during pregnancy, and disruption of the fetomaternal tolerance can result in preterm labor (Gomez-Lopez et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gomez-Lopez et al., 2014.

claim: Disruption of fetomaternal tolerance can result in preterm labor.
source: Fetomaternal immune tolerance is essential to suppress rejection during pregnancy, and disruption of the fetomaternal tolerance can result in preterm labor (Gomez-Lopez et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gomez-Lopez et al., 2014.

claim: During the perinatal period, newborns transition from their dependence on maternal immunity to their own immune system.
source: During the perinatal period, newborns transition from their dependence on maternal immunity to their own immune system (Simon et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Simon et al., 2015.

claim: Rapid exposure to environmental assaults, such as microbes, after birth renders neonates susceptible to infections.
source: Rapid exposure to environmental assaults, such as microbes, after birth renders neonates susceptible to infections (MacGillivray and Kollmann, 2014; Kollmann et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to MacGillivray and Kollmann, 2014 and Kollmann et al., 2017.

claim: Most pediatric vaccines need to be administered four times during the first 15 months of age in order to elicit adult like protective immunity against infections.
source: Although vaccination has been successful in curbing early age infection rates, infants are still vulnerable during to first year of life, especially because most pediatric vaccines need to be administered four times during the first 15 months of age in order to elicit adult like protective immunity against infections (Ehreth, 2003; Jacobson, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ehreth, 2003 and Jacobson, 2020.

claim: The exact reasons for the suboptimal vaccine responses after birth are not sufficiently delineated.
source: The exact reasons for the suboptimal vaccine responses after birth are not sufficiently delineated and this knowledge gap is an obstacle in improving pediatric vaccines (Kollmann et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kollmann et al., 2017.

claim: The protective host response to most vaccines is initiated by the recognition of vaccine antigen via the B cell receptor (BCR).
source: The protective host response to most vaccines is initiated by the recognition of vaccine antigen via the B cell receptor (BCR) (Akkaya et al., 2020), followed by the generation of germinal center (GC) response that involve follicular helper T (Tfh) cells and GC B cells in secondary lymphoid organs (Vinuesa et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Akkaya et al., 2020.

claim: The protective host response to most vaccines involves the generation of germinal center (GC) response that involve follicular helper T (Tfh) cells and GC B cells in secondary lymphoid organs.
source: The protective host response to most vaccines is initiated by the recognition of vaccine antigen via the B cell receptor (BCR) (Akkaya et al., 2020), followed by the generation of germinal center (GC) response that involve follicular helper T (Tfh) cells and GC B cells in secondary lymphoid organs (Vinuesa et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Vinuesa et al., 2016.

claim: The unique properties of impaired Tfh response contribute to the weak immune response to vaccines in neonatal mice.
source: We and others have shown that the unique properties of impaired Tfh response contribute to the weak immune response to vaccines in neonatal mice (Mastelic et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mastelic et al., 2012 and Yang et al., 2018.

claim: Several types of immune suppressive cells contribute to fetomaternal immune tolerance and to human and murine neonatal suboptimal immunity via the potent anti-inflammatory cytokine interleukin (IL)–10.
source: In addition, several types of immune suppressive cells contribute to fetomaternal immune tolerance and to human and murine neonatal suboptimal immunity via the potent anti-inflammatory cytokine interleukin (IL)–10 (Kollmann et al., 2017; Basha et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kollmann et al., 2017 and Basha et al., 2014.

claim: IL-10 was initially described as a function of activated CD4+ T helper (Th) 2 cells to inhibit cytokine production by Th1 cells.
source: Initially described as a function of activated CD4+ T helper (Th) 2 cells to inhibit cytokine production by Th1 cells (Fiorentino et al., 1989), IL-10 has subsequently been shown to be produced by different cell types including dendritic cells, macrophages, neutrophils, mast cells, natural killer cells, T cells, and B cells (Moore et al., 2001; Ouyang and O'Garra, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fiorentino et al., 1989.

claim: IL-10 has been shown to be produced by different cell types including dendritic cells, macrophages, neutrophils, mast cells, natural killer cells, T cells, and B cells.
source: Initially described as a function of activated CD4+ T helper (Th) 2 cells to inhibit cytokine production by Th1 cells (Fiorentino et al., 1989), IL-10 has subsequently been shown to be produced by different cell types including dendritic cells, macrophages, neutrophils, mast cells, natural killer cells, T cells, and B cells (Moore et al., 2001; Ouyang and O'Garra, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Moore et al., 2001 and Ouyang and O'Garra, 2019.

claim: The main activity of IL-10 is the inhibition of inflammatory responses by both the innate and the adaptive immune cells.
source: The main activity of IL-10 is the inhibition of inflammatory responses (e.g., pro-inflammatory cytokine and chemokine synthesis, nitric oxide production, and antigen presentation) by both the innate and the adaptive immune cells (Moore et al., 2001; Ouyang and O'Garra, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Moore et al., 2001 and Ouyang and O'Garra, 2019.

claim: IL-10 expression is controlled by various transcription factors including nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB), signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3), and GATA binding protein 3 (GATA3) depending on the upstream signaling pathways and cell types.
source: IL-10 expression is controlled by various transcription factors including nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB), signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3), and GATA binding protein 3 (GATA3) depending on the upstream signaling pathways and cell types (Saraiva and O'Garra, 2010; Hedrich and Bream, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Saraiva and O'Garra, 2010 and Hedrich and Bream, 2010.

claim: In human and neonatal B cells, IL-10 production has been shown to be mediated by BCR engagement.
source: In human and neonatal B cells, IL-10 production has been shown to be mediated by a range of signaling, including BCR engagement (Alhakeem et al., 2015), CD40 ligand (Burdin et al., 1997), TLR agonists (Lampropoulou et al., 2008), IL-1β, IL-6 (Rosser et al., 2014) and type I interferons (Zhang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Alhakeem et al., 2015.

claim: In human and neonatal B cells, IL-10 production has been shown to be mediated by CD40 ligand.
source: In human and neonatal B cells, IL-10 production has been shown to be mediated by a range of signaling, including BCR engagement (Alhakeem et al., 2015), CD40 ligand (Burdin et al., 1997), TLR agonists (Lampropoulou et al., 2008), IL-1β, IL-6 (Rosser et al., 2014) and type I interferons (Zhang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Burdin et al., 1997.

claim: In human and neonatal B cells, IL-10 production has been shown to be mediated by TLR agonists.
source: In human and neonatal B cells, IL-10 production has been shown to be mediated by a range of signaling, including BCR engagement (Alhakeem et al., 2015), CD40 ligand (Burdin et al., 1997), TLR agonists (Lampropoulou et al., 2008), IL-1β, IL-6 (Rosser et al., 2014) and type I interferons (Zhang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lampropoulou et al., 2008.

claim: In human and neonatal B cells, IL-10 production has been shown to be mediated by IL-1β and IL-6.
source: In human and neonatal B cells, IL-10 production has been shown to be mediated by a range of signaling, including BCR engagement (Alhakeem et al., 2015), CD40 ligand (Burdin et al., 1997), TLR agonists (Lampropoulou et al., 2008), IL-1β, IL-6 (Rosser et al., 2014) and type I interferons (Zhang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rosser et al., 2014.

claim: In human and neonatal B cells, IL-10 production has been shown to be mediated by type I interferons.
source: In human and neonatal B cells, IL-10 production has been shown to be mediated by a range of signaling, including BCR engagement (Alhakeem et al., 2015), CD40 ligand (Burdin et al., 1997), TLR agonists (Lampropoulou et al., 2008), IL-1β, IL-6 (Rosser et al., 2014) and type I interferons (Zhang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2007.

claim: B cells can be divided into two subsets: CD43+ B-1 cells and CD43- non B-1 cells which include follicular B-2 cells, marginal zone B cells and IL-10 producing regulatory B cells (Bregs).
source: B cells can be divided into two subsets: CD43+ B-1 cells and CD43- non B-1 cells which include follicular B-2 cells, marginal zone B cells and IL-10 producing regulatory B cells (Bregs) (Baumgarth, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Baumgarth, 2011.

claim: B-1 cells are further subdivided into innate-like B-1a (CD5+) cells and B-1b (CD5-) cells.
source: B-1 cells are further subdivided into innate-like B-1a (CD5+) cells and B-1b (CD5-) cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about B cell classification.

claim: B-1 cells emerge from the liver in the very early stage of life and have been suggested to be maintained by a 'self-renewal' process.
source: After emerging from the liver in the very early stage of life, B-1 cells have been suggested to be maintained by a 'self-renewal' process, whereas B-2 cells are continuously produced from progenitors in the bone marrow after birth in mice and humans (Baumgarth, 2011; Montecino-Rodriguez and Dorshkind, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Baumgarth, 2011 and Montecino-Rodriguez and Dorshkind, 2012.

claim: B-2 cells are continuously produced from progenitors in the bone marrow after birth in mice and humans.
source: After emerging from the liver in the very early stage of life, B-1 cells have been suggested to be maintained by a 'self-renewal' process, whereas B-2 cells are continuously produced from progenitors in the bone marrow after birth in mice and humans (Baumgarth, 2011; Montecino-Rodriguez and Dorshkind, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Baumgarth, 2011 and Montecino-Rodriguez and Dorshkind, 2012.

claim: Murine B-1 cells dominate the B cell population in neonatal spleen (30% of IgM+ splenic B cells).
source: Accordingly, murine B-1 cells, which dominate the B cell population in neonatal spleen (30% of IgM+ splenic B cells), are gradually exceeded by B-2 cells with age and account for approximately 2% in adult splenic B cells (Hayakawa et al., 1983; Montecino-Rodriguez and Dorshkind, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hayakawa et al., 1983 and Montecino-Rodriguez and Dorshkind, 2011.

claim: Murine B-1 cells are gradually exceeded by B-2 cells with age and account for approximately 2% in adult splenic B cells.
source: Accordingly, murine B-1 cells, which dominate the B cell population in neonatal spleen (30% of IgM+ splenic B cells), are gradually exceeded by B-2 cells with age and account for approximately 2% in adult splenic B cells (Hayakawa et al., 1983; Montecino-Rodriguez and Dorshkind, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hayakawa et al., 1983 and Montecino-Rodriguez and Dorshkind, 2011.

claim: Among the B cells, B-1 cells are the main producers of IL-10.
source: Among the B cells, B-1 cells are the main producers of IL-10 (O'Garra et al., 1992; Zhang, 2013) and since B-1 cells account for 1/3 of neonatal mouse spleen, they are considered as the main source of IL-10 in neonatal spleen.
evidence: This is supported by citations to O'Garra et al., 1992 and Zhang, 2013.

claim: B-1 cells are considered as the main source of IL-10 in neonatal spleen because they account for 1/3 of neonatal mouse spleen.
source: Among the B cells, B-1 cells are the main producers of IL-10 (O'Garra et al., 1992; Zhang, 2013) and since B-1 cells account for 1/3 of neonatal mouse spleen, they are considered as the main source of IL-10 in neonatal spleen.
evidence: This is an inference based on the proportion of B-1 cells and their IL-10 production capacity.

claim: Both mouse neonatal splenic and human cord blood Breg cells manifest suppressive activity.
source: Both mouse neonatal splenic and human cord blood Breg cells are shown to manifest suppressive activity (Zhang, 2013; Sarvaria et al., 2016; Esteve-Solé et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zhang, 2013; Sarvaria et al., 2016; and Esteve-Solé et al., 2017.

claim: Purified neonatal splenic CD19+CD43- cells produced higher IL-10 than adult counterparts after stimulation with anti-IgM antibodies.
source: As observed in the flow cytometry analysis of gated CD19+CD43- cells (Figure 1B), purified neonatal CD19+CD43- cells also produced higher IL-10 than the adult counterparts (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: The increase in IL-10 production by neonatal CD19+CD43- cells reached statistical significance at 6-hr time point and remained high after peaking at 12 hr.
source: The increase in IL-10 production reached statistical significance at 6-hr time point and remained high after peaking at 12 hr.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: IL-10 production by adult CD19+CD43- cells was minimal at all time points.
source: IL-10 production by adult CD19+CD43- cells was minimal at all time points.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Adult CD19+CD43- cells manifested a rapid and sharp increase in Il10 expression which was quickly shut off within 6 hr post-stimulation.
source: Il10 mRNA measurement indicated that adult CD19+CD43- cells manifested a rapid and sharp increase in Il10 expression which was quickly shut off within 6 hr post-stimulation (Figure 1D), and this temporal gene expression appeared to be insufficient for IL-10 protein synthesis (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and 1C.

claim: The temporal Il10 gene expression in adult CD19+CD43- cells appeared to be insufficient for IL-10 protein synthesis.
source: Il10 mRNA measurement indicated that adult CD19+CD43- cells manifested a rapid and sharp increase in Il10 expression which was quickly shut off within 6 hr post-stimulation (Figure 1D), and this temporal gene expression appeared to be insufficient for IL-10 protein synthesis (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of mRNA and protein data in Figures 1D and 1C.

claim: Neonatal CD19+CD43- cells showed an initial sharp increase of Il10 expression that further increased at later time points, facilitating the production of IL-10.
source: An initial sharp increase of Il10 expression was also observed in neonatal CD19+CD43- cells (Figure 1D). Unlike in adult cells, neonatal Il10 expression further increased at later time points, facilitating the production of IL-10 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1D and 1C.

claim: Neonatal spleen contained higher percentage of CD43+ B-1 cells than adult spleen.
source: Also confirming previous reports (Hayakawa et al., 1983; Sun et al., 2005), neonatal spleen contained higher percentage of CD43+ B-1 cells than adult spleen (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B, and citations to Hayakawa et al., 1983 and Sun et al., 2005.

claim: Neonatal CD43+ cells contained higher percentage of CD19+IL-10+ B cells than adult cells prior to BCR stimulation.
source: Further gating of purified B cells based on CD43 expression indicated that neonatal CD43+ cells contained higher percentage of CD19+IL-10+ B cells than adult cells prior to BCR stimulation and there was a modest increase after BCR stimulation in both the age groups (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: There was a modest increase in CD19+IL-10+ B cells in CD43+ population after BCR stimulation in both adult and neonatal age groups.
source: Further gating of purified B cells based on CD43 expression indicated that neonatal CD43+ cells contained higher percentage of CD19+IL-10+ B cells than adult cells prior to BCR stimulation and there was a modest increase after BCR stimulation in both the age groups (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: BCR stimulation induced a significant increase in IL-10+ cells among the neonatal CD43- population.
source: Unlike the CD43+ population, BCR stimulation induced a significant increase in IL-10+ cells among the neonatal CD43- population, whereas IL-10+ cells remained low in adult CD43- population after BCR-stimulation (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: IL-10+ cells remained low in adult CD43- population after BCR-stimulation.
source: Unlike the CD43+ population, BCR stimulation induced a significant increase in IL-10+ cells among the neonatal CD43- population, whereas IL-10+ cells remained low in adult CD43- population after BCR-stimulation (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: There was no statistically significant difference in the CD43 MFI between adult and neonatal mice after the purification of CD19+CD43- cells.
source: There was no statistically significant difference in the CD43 MFI between adult and neonatal mice after the purification of CD19+CD43- cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A and B.

claim: There was no significant difference in the expression of spn gene coding for CD43 between purified adult and neonatal CD19+CD43- cells.
source: Furthermore, there was no significant difference in the expression of spn gene coding for CD43 between purified adult and neonatal CD19+CD43- cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4C.

claim: Elevated levels of membrane IgM have been observed in human cord blood B cells compared to adult cells.
source: Elevated levels of membrane IgM have been observed in human cord blood B cells compared to adult cells (Glaesener et al., 2018; Macardle et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Glaesener et al., 2018 and Macardle et al., 1997.

claim: There was no statistically significant difference in the percentage of CD19+IgM+ cells between adults and neonates.
source: There was no statistically significant difference in the percentage of CD19+IgM+ cells between adults and neonates, although neonates exhibited significantly lower frequency of CD19+IgD+ B cells compared to adults (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A, B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5A, B.

claim: Neonates exhibited significantly lower frequency of CD19+IgD+ B cells compared to adults.
source: There was no statistically significant difference in the percentage of CD19+IgM+ cells between adults and neonates, although neonates exhibited significantly lower frequency of CD19+IgD+ B cells compared to adults (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A, B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5A, B.

claim: Neonatal CD19+CD43- cells showed higher frequency and MFI of IgMhi cells compared to adult counterparts.
source: When we analyzed the subsets, we found that neonatal CD19+CD43- cells showed higher frequency and MFI of IgMhi cells compared to adult counterparts, whereas IgM levels were statistically comparable between adult and neonatal CD43+ B-1 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5A.

claim: IgM levels were statistically comparable between adult and neonatal CD43+ B-1 cells.
source: When we analyzed the subsets, we found that neonatal CD19+CD43- cells showed higher frequency and MFI of IgMhi cells compared to adult counterparts, whereas IgM levels were statistically comparable between adult and neonatal CD43+ B-1 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5A.

claim: Both neonatal CD19+CD43- cells and CD43+ B-1 cells exhibited lower frequency and MFI of IgDhi cells compared to adult counterparts.
source: Both neonatal CD19+CD43- cells and CD43+ B-1 cells exhibited lower frequency and MFI of IgDhi cells compared to adult counterparts.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5B.

claim: Anti-IgM antibodies may alter the expression of CD43.
source: Because our experimental set up relies on the separation of CD43- cells, we wanted to assess the changes in CD43 expression before and after stimulation since anti-IgM antibodies may alter the expression of CD43 (Björck et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Björck et al., 1991.

claim: Unstimulated adult CD19+ cells contained only a small population of CD43+ cells which were approximately 1/5th of the neonatal CD43+ cells.
source: We observed that unstimulated adult CD19+ cells contained only a small population of CD43+ cells which were approximately 1/5th of the neonatal CD43+ cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: In both age groups, CD43+ cell population increased after BCR engagement.
source: In both age groups, CD43+ cell population increased after BCR engagement.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: The frequencies of T2-MZP were significantly lower in neonatal spleen than in adult spleen.
source: We found that the frequencies of T2-MZP (Figure 1—figure supplement 7A) and MZB (Figure 1—figure supplement 7B) were significantly lower in neonatal spleen than in adult spleen, and the Tim-1 B cell population was comparable between the two age groups (Figure 1—figure supplement 7C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7A.

claim: The frequencies of MZB were significantly lower in neonatal spleen than in adult spleen.
source: We found that the frequencies of T2-MZP (Figure 1—figure supplement 7A) and MZB (Figure 1—figure supplement 7B) were significantly lower in neonatal spleen than in adult spleen, and the Tim-1 B cell population was comparable between the two age groups (Figure 1—figure supplement 7C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7B.

claim: The Tim-1 B cell population was comparable between adult and neonatal age groups.
source: We found that the frequencies of T2-MZP (Figure 1—figure supplement 7A) and MZB (Figure 1—figure supplement 7B) were significantly lower in neonatal spleen than in adult spleen, and the Tim-1 B cell population was comparable between the two age groups (Figure 1—figure supplement 7C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7C.

claim: Adult B10 cells were first described as splenic CD19+ cells expressing CD5 and CD1dhi.
source: Adult B10 cells with T cell suppressive properties were first described by Yanaba and colleagues as splenic CD19+ cells expressing CD5 and CD1dhi (Yanaba et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yanaba et al., 2008.

claim: The frequencies of CD5+CD1d+ as well as CD5+CD1dhi populations were significantly more in neonates than in adults.
source: Our data indicated that the frequencies of CD5+CD1d+ as well as CD5+CD1dhi populations were significantly more in neonates than in adults (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The larger population of B10 cells in neonates was attributed to the significantly higher expression of CD5.
source: Assessment of changes in the expression of individual surface markers revealed that the larger population of B10 cells in neonates was attributed to the significantly higher expression of CD5 (Figure 1—figure supplement 8A) rather than a difference in CD1d expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 8B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 8A and 8B.

claim: Adult and neonatal CD5+CD1d+ cells were the main producers of IL-10 after stimulation of CD19+CD43- cells with anti-IgM antibody.
source: After stimulation of CD19+CD43- cells with anti-IgM antibody, adult and neonatal CD5+CD1d+ cells were the main producers of IL-10, but the neonatal CD5+CD1d+IL-10+ population was higher than the adult counterparts (Figure 1—figure supplement 9A–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 9A–D.

claim: The neonatal CD5+CD1d+IL-10+ population was higher than the adult counterparts after anti-IgM stimulation.
source: After stimulation of CD19+CD43- cells with anti-IgM antibody, adult and neonatal CD5+CD1d+ cells were the main producers of IL-10, but the neonatal CD5+CD1d+IL-10+ population was higher than the adult counterparts (Figure 1—figure supplement 9A–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 9A–D.

claim: IL-10-producing population was higher when the cells were further gated for B10 (CD5+CD1hi) population in both age groups.
source: IL-10-producing population was even higher when the cells were further gated for B10 (CD5+CD1hi) population in both age groups (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The frequency as well as the MFI of IL-10-producing B10 population was more in neonatal mice than those in adult mice.
source: Once again, the frequency as well as the MFI of IL-10-producing B10 population was more in neonatal mice then those in adult mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: There were 1341 increased and 1905 decreased genes in adult B cells following BCR engagement.
source: There were 1341 increased and 1905 decreased genes in adult B cells compared to 716 increased and 962 decreased genes in neonatal B cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: There were 716 increased and 962 decreased genes in neonatal B cells following BCR engagement.
source: There were 1341 increased and 1905 decreased genes in adult B cells compared to 716 increased and 962 decreased genes in neonatal B cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The top gene sets enriched in neonatal CD19+CD43- cells after anti-IgM stimulation contained cytokine receptor signaling and STAT protein-related signaling pathways.
source: The top gene sets enriched in neonatal CD19+CD43- cells after anti-IgM stimulation contained cytokine receptor signaling and STAT protein-related signaling pathways (O'Shea et al., 2013), whereas the gene sets involved in biological processes as well as the signaling pathways controlled by mitogen-activated protein kinases (MAPKs) and Akt (O'Shea et al., 2013; Buj and Aird, 2018; Rosini et al., 2000; Van Laethem et al., 2004; Zhuang et al., 2016) were highly ranked in adult CD19+CD43- cells.
evidence: This is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 2A and citations.

claim: Gene sets involved in biological processes as well as the signaling pathways controlled by MAPKs and Akt were highly ranked in adult CD19+CD43- cells after anti-IgM stimulation.
source: The top gene sets enriched in neonatal CD19+CD43- cells after anti-IgM stimulation contained cytokine receptor signaling and STAT protein-related signaling pathways (O'Shea et al., 2013), whereas the gene sets involved in biological processes as well as the signaling pathways controlled by mitogen-activated protein kinases (MAPKs) and Akt (O'Shea et al., 2013; Buj and Aird, 2018; Rosini et al., 2000; Van Laethem et al., 2004; Zhuang et al., 2016) were highly ranked in adult CD19+CD43- cells.
evidence: This is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 2A and citations.

claim: Target genes for STAT3, STAT5A, and STAT5B were highly expressed in anti-IgM-stimulated neonatal B cells.
source: This analysis revealed that target genes for STAT3, STAT5A, and STAT5B were highly expressed in anti-IgM-stimulated neonatal B cells, suggesting that these STAT proteins were activated in neonatal CD19+CD43- cells after BCR engagement (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: STAT3, STAT5A, and STAT5B were activated in neonatal CD19+CD43- cells after BCR engagement.
source: This analysis revealed that target genes for STAT3, STAT5A, and STAT5B were highly expressed in anti-IgM-stimulated neonatal B cells, suggesting that these STAT proteins were activated in neonatal CD19+CD43- cells after BCR engagement (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression of target genes shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Target genes for MAPK and Akt signaling pathway-activated transcription factors such as MYC, ELK1, and AP-1 were not expressed in neonatal CD19+CD43- cells compared to adult cells.
source: Supporting the findings in C5 gene ontology analysis, target genes for MAPK and Akt signaling pathway-activated transcription factors such as MYC, ELK1, and AP-1 (Zhang and Liu, 2002; Hoxhaj and Manning, 2020) were not expressed in neonatal CD19+CD43- cells compared to adult cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 2B and citations.

claim: STAT3 and STAT5 were highly phosphorylated in neonatal B cells after BCR stimulation.
source: We found that STAT3 and STAT5 were highly phosphorylated in neonatal B cells although their activation kinetics was different (Figure 2C, D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2C and 2D.

claim: STAT5 phosphorylation was detected as early as 5 min and peaked at 15 min after BCR crosslinking.
source: STAT5 phosphorylation was detected as early as 5 min and peaked at 15 min after BCR crosslinking (Figure 2C), whereas STAT3 phosphorylation peaked at around 4 hr post-stimulation (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: STAT3 phosphorylation peaked at around 4 hr post-stimulation after BCR crosslinking.
source: STAT5 phosphorylation was detected as early as 5 min and peaked at 15 min after BCR crosslinking (Figure 2C), whereas STAT3 phosphorylation peaked at around 4 hr post-stimulation (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: STAT1 phosphorylation was not observed after BCR cross-linking in either adult or neonatal B cells.
source: In addition, STAT1 phosphorylation was not observed after BCR cross-linking in either adult or neonatal B cells, while STAT1 was phosphorylated in B cells stimulated with recombinant IL-21 (Figure 2C, D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2), suggesting that STAT1 was not activated by BCR and that the marker genes were expressed independently of STAT1.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2C, 2D, and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: STAT1 was phosphorylated in B cells stimulated with recombinant IL-21.
source: In addition, STAT1 phosphorylation was not observed after BCR cross-linking in either adult or neonatal B cells, while STAT1 was phosphorylated in B cells stimulated with recombinant IL-21 (Figure 2C, D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2), suggesting that STAT1 was not activated by BCR and that the marker genes were expressed independently of STAT1.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: STAT1 was not activated by BCR.
source: In addition, STAT1 phosphorylation was not observed after BCR cross-linking in either adult or neonatal B cells, while STAT1 was phosphorylated in B cells stimulated with recombinant IL-21 (Figure 2C, D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2), suggesting that STAT1 was not activated by BCR and that the marker genes were expressed independently of STAT1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of STAT1 phosphorylation after BCR stimulation.

claim: Akt, p38, JNK and ERK were phosphorylated in adult B cells, but not in neonatal cells after BCR stimulation.
source: Confirming the GSEA analysis data, Akt, p38, JNK and ERK were phosphorylated in adult B cells, but not in neonatal cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Both S3I-201 (STAT3 inhibitor) and Pimozide (STAT5 inhibitor) inhibited BCR-induced Il10 mRNA expression and IL-10 protein production.
source: We found that both S3I-201 (STAT3 inhibitor) and Pimozide (STAT5 inhibitor) inhibited BCR-induced Il10 mRNA expression and IL-10 protein production (Figure 3A, B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: Pyridone 6 effectively inhibited STAT3 and STAT5 phosphorylations induced by IL-6 and IL-21, respectively.
source: We first verified the inhibitory activity of Pyridone 6 in B cells, which effectively inhibited STAT3 and STAT5 phosphorylations induced by IL-6 and IL-21, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: When neonatal B cells were stimulated through BCR in the presence of Pyridone 6, STAT3 phosphorylation, but not STAT5 phosphorylation, was completely suppressed.
source: When neonatal B cells were stimulated through BCR in the presence of Pyridone 6, STAT3 phosphorylation, but not STAT5 phosphorylation, was completely suppressed (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Specific JAK2 inhibitor AG490 failed to inhibit STAT5 phosphorylation.
source: Similarly, as previously observed (Wang et al., 2007), specific JAK2 inhibitor AG490 failed to inhibit STAT5 phosphorylation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and a citation to Wang et al., 2007.

claim: Neonatal BCR-induced STAT5 activation was inhibited by Ibrutinib (Bruton's tyrosine kinase (BTK) inhibitor) and Staurosporine (protein kinase C (PKC) inhibitor).
source: While neonatal BCR-induced STAT5 activation was JAK-independent, it was inhibited by Ibrutinib (Bruton's tyrosine kinase (BTK) inhibitor) and Staurosporine (protein kinase C (PKC) inhibitor) as shown previously (Karras et al., 1996; Mahajan et al., 2001; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and citations to Karras et al., 1996 and Mahajan et al., 2001.

claim: BCR induced STAT3 phosphorylation relied on JAKs.
source: These results suggested that whereas BCR induced STAT3 phosphorylation relied on JAKs, STAT5 is activated in a JAK-independent and BTK/PKC-dependent fashion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the inhibitor experiments shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: STAT5 is activated in a JAK-independent and BTK/PKC-dependent fashion.
source: These results suggested that whereas BCR induced STAT3 phosphorylation relied on JAKs, STAT5 is activated in a JAK-independent and BTK/PKC-dependent fashion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the inhibitor experiments shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Pimozide suppressed neonatal BCR-induced STAT3 phosphorylation.
source: Supporting this hypothesis and suggesting that STAT5 functions as an upstream mediator of STAT3, Pimozide suppressed neonatal BCR-induced STAT3 phosphorylation (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: STAT5 functions as an upstream mediator of STAT3.
source: Supporting this hypothesis and suggesting that STAT5 functions as an upstream mediator of STAT3, Pimozide suppressed neonatal BCR-induced STAT3 phosphorylation (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is an inference based on the effect of Pimozide shown in Figure 3D.

claim: There was significantly higher Il6 mRNA expression and IL-6 protein production following BCR cross-linking in neonatal CD19+CD43- B cells compared to those in adult counterparts.
source: Indeed, we found significantly higher Il6 mRNA expression and IL-6 protein production following BCR cross-linking in neonatal CD19+CD43- B cells compared to those in adult counterparts (Figure 3E, F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and 3F.

claim: Higher IL-6 production in neonatal B cells following BCR cross-linking was also observed by flow cytometry.
source: Higher IL-6 production in neonatal B cells following BCR cross-linking was also observed by flow cytometry (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: STAT5 can contribute to IL-6 promoter activity in macrophages and cell lines.
source: While BCR-mediated signaling alone is not sufficient to induce IL-6 in adult B cells (Kenny et al., 2013; Arkatkar et al., 2017), studies in macrophages and cell lines have shown that STAT5 can contribute to IL-6 promoter activity (Kawashima et al., 2001; Kimura et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kawashima et al., 2001 and Kimura et al., 2005.

claim: Pimozide abrogated both Il6 mRNA expression and IL-6 protein production following BCR engagement.
source: Indeed, Pimozide abrogated both Il6 mRNA expression and IL-6 protein production following BCR engagement, whereas the pan-JAK inhibitor Pyridone 6 did not (Figure 3G, H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G and 3H.

claim: The pan-JAK inhibitor Pyridone 6 did not abrogate Il6 mRNA expression and IL-6 protein production following BCR engagement.
source: Indeed, Pimozide abrogated both Il6 mRNA expression and IL-6 protein production following BCR engagement, whereas the pan-JAK inhibitor Pyridone 6 did not (Figure 3G, H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G and 3H.

claim: Small interfering RNA targeting STAT5 suppressed BCR-induced IL-6 production.
source: This result was reproduced by using small interfering RNA targeting STAT5, which also suppressed BCR-induced IL-6 production (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: STAT5 has an essential role in the production of IL-6 by BCR-activated neonatal CD19+CD43- cells.
source: These findings indicated that STAT5 has an essential role in the production of IL-6 by BCR-activated neonatal CD19+CD43- cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the inhibitor and siRNA experiments shown in Figures 3G, 3H, and 3I.

claim: IL-6 signaling is mediated by membrane-bound or soluble IL-6 receptor alpha (IL-6Rα) and a transmembrane protein gp130.
source: IL-6 signaling is mediated by membrane-bound or soluble IL-6 receptor alpha (IL-6Rα) and a transmembrane protein gp130 (Su et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Su et al., 2017.

claim: Only after forming a complex with IL-6, the IL-6Rα associates with gp130 and transduces signals for JAK-STAT3 pathway.
source: Only after forming a complex with IL-6, the IL-6Rα associates with gp130 and transduces signals for JAK-STAT3 pathway (Taga et al., 1989; Murakami et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Taga et al., 1989 and Murakami et al., 1993.

claim: Blockade of IL-6 signaling with anti-IL-6Rα monoclonal antibody (15A7) reduced neonatal BCR-induced STAT3 phosphorylation, but not STAT5 phosphorylation.
source: Suggesting a role for IL-6 in STAT3 activation, blockade of IL-6 signaling with anti-IL-6Rα monoclonal antibody (15A7) reduced neonatal BCR-induced STAT3 phosphorylation, but not STAT5 phosphorylation (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The gp130 inhibitor SC144 abrogated STAT3 phosphorylation following BCR engagement.
source: Similarly, the gp130 inhibitor SC144 abrogated STAT3 phosphorylation following BCR engagement (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: STAT3 is activated by IL-10 signaling.
source: While the blocking experiments indicated that IL-6 produced in response to BCR-engagement was responsible for STAT3 activation, STAT3 is also activated by IL-10 signaling (Shouval et al., 2014; Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Shouval et al., 2014 and experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Anti-IL-10R antibody did not reduce neonatal BCR-induced STAT3 phosphorylation while anti-IL-6Rα antibody did.
source: We found that anti-IL-10R antibody did not reduce neonatal BCR-induced STAT3 phosphorylation while anti-IL-6Rα antibody did (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Neonatal CD19+CD43- cells produced IL-6 following BCR cross-linking in a STAT5-dependent manner.
source: These results suggest that neonatal CD19+CD43- cells produced IL-6 following BCR cross-linking in a STAT5-dependent manner, and subsequently the secreted IL-6 activated STAT3 via the IL-6R-gp130 pathway in an autocrine/paracrine fashion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The secreted IL-6 activated STAT3 via the IL-6R-gp130 pathway in an autocrine/paracrine fashion.
source: These results suggest that neonatal CD19+CD43- cells produced IL-6 following BCR cross-linking in a STAT5-dependent manner, and subsequently the secreted IL-6 activated STAT3 via the IL-6R-gp130 pathway in an autocrine/paracrine fashion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Blocking with antibodies against IL-6Rα, but not with anti-IL-10R, totally abrogated Il10 mRNA expression 7 hr after BCR stimulation.
source: We found that blocking with antibodies against IL-6Rα, but not with anti-IL-10R, totally abrogated Il10 mRNA expression 7 hr after BCR stimulation (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: BCR cross-linking did not induce STAT3 phosphorylation in CD19+CD43- cells from IL-6 KO neonatal mice.
source: Further underscoring the dependency of BCR-induced STAT3 activation on IL-6 production, BCR cross-linking did not induce STAT3 phosphorylation in CD19+CD43- cells from IL-6 KO neonatal mice, whereas STAT5 phosphorylation was comparable between wild-type and IL-6 KO strains (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: STAT5 phosphorylation was comparable between wild-type and IL-6 KO strains.
source: Further underscoring the dependency of BCR-induced STAT3 activation on IL-6 production, BCR cross-linking did not induce STAT3 phosphorylation in CD19+CD43- cells from IL-6 KO neonatal mice, whereas STAT5 phosphorylation was comparable between wild-type and IL-6 KO strains (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Recombinant IL-6 induced the phosphorylation of STAT3 in IL-6 KO neonatal CD19+CD43- cells.
source: We excluded the possibility of a defect in STAT3 activation in IL-6-deficient CD19+CD43- cells because recombinant IL-6 induced the phosphorylation of STAT3 in IL-6 KO neonatal CD19+CD43- cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Both Il10 gene expression and IL-10 protein levels were significantly reduced in IL-6 KO neonatal CD19+CD43- cells compared to wild-type counterparts.
source: Both Il10 gene expression and IL-10 protein levels were significantly reduced in IL-6 KO neonatal CD19+CD43- cells compared to wild-type counterparts (Figure 4, D and E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D and 4E.

claim: Both Tnf gene expression and TNF-α protein levels were comparable between wild-type and IL-6-deficient neonatal CD19+CD43- cells.
source: IL-6 deficiency did not create an overall suppressive state because both Tnf gene expression and TNF-α protein levels were comparable between wild-type and IL-6-deficient neonatal CD19+CD43- cells (Figure 4, D and E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D and 4E.

claim: Neonatal CD19+CD43- cells significantly increased Il1b gene expression following BCR cross-linking.
source: While neonatal CD19+CD43- cells significantly increased Il1b gene expression following BCR cross-linking (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A), blocking IL-1β signaling using a neutralizing antibody failed to reduce IL-10 production by IL-6-deficient neonatal CD19+CD43- B cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B, C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Blocking IL-1β signaling using a neutralizing antibody failed to reduce IL-10 production by IL-6-deficient neonatal CD19+CD43- B cells.
source: While neonatal CD19+CD43- cells significantly increased Il1b gene expression following BCR cross-linking (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A), blocking IL-1β signaling using a neutralizing antibody failed to reduce IL-10 production by IL-6-deficient neonatal CD19+CD43- B cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B, C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3B and 3C.

claim: Biologically active recombinant IL-1β did not induce IL-10 while recombinant IL-6 did.
source: In addition, biologically active recombinant IL-1β (Figure 4—figure supplement 3D) did not induce IL-10 while recombinant IL-6 did (Figure 4—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3D and 3E.

claim: IL-35 production was not observed following BCR cross-linking.
source: Ruling out its involvement, IL-35 production was not observed following BCR cross-linking (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Neonatal B cells expressed modest but significantly higher levels of surface IL-6Rα compared to their adult counterpart.
source: In addition to the elevated IL-6 production, flow cytometry assessment revealed that neonatal B cells expressed modest but significantly higher levels of surface IL-6Rα compared to their adult counterpart (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The expression level of gp130 was comparable between adult and neonatal age groups.
source: The expression level of gp130 was comparable between the two age groups (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: P-STAT3 was detected in neonatal cells with as little as 0.04 ng/mL of IL-6.
source: We detected P-STAT3 in neonatal cells with as little as 0.04 ng/mL of IL-6 whereas approximately 62 times more IL-6 (2.5 ng/mL) was needed to induce the phosphorylation of STAT3 in adult cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Approximately 62 times more IL-6 (2.5 ng/mL) was needed to induce the phosphorylation of STAT3 in adult cells compared to neonatal cells.
source: We detected P-STAT3 in neonatal cells with as little as 0.04 ng/mL of IL-6 whereas approximately 62 times more IL-6 (2.5 ng/mL) was needed to induce the phosphorylation of STAT3 in adult cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The EC50 for neonatal B cells (0.98±0.41 ng/mL) was significantly lower than that for adult counterparts (4.37±1.27 ng/mL).
source: Quantification of the IL-6 activity by computing half maximal effective concentration (EC50) indicated that the EC50 for neonatal B cells (0.98±0.41 ng/mL) was significantly lower than that for adult counterparts (4.37±1.27 ng/mL).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The elevated neonatal B cell P-STAT3 activity translated into increased IL-10 production in IL-6-stimulated neonatal CD19+CD43- cells.
source: Moreover, the elevated neonatal B cell P-STAT3 activity translated into increased IL-10 production in IL-6-stimulated neonatal CD19+CD43- cells (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: IL-10 secreted by IL-6-deficient neonatal CD19+CD43- cells were comparable to that from wild-type neonatal CD19+CD43- cells in response to CpG and lipopolysaccharide (LPS).
source: IL-10 secreted by IL-6-deficient neonatal CD19+CD43- cells were comparable to that from wild-type neonatal CD19+CD43- cells in response to CpG and lipopolysaccharide (LPS), suggesting that TLR signaling-induced IL-10 production was not dependent on IL-6.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: TLR signaling-induced IL-10 production was not dependent on IL-6.
source: IL-10 secreted by IL-6-deficient neonatal CD19+CD43- cells were comparable to that from wild-type neonatal CD19+CD43- cells in response to CpG and lipopolysaccharide (LPS), suggesting that TLR signaling-induced IL-10 production was not dependent on IL-6.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: BCR cross-linking increased the phosphorylation of PKC in neonatal CD19+CD43- cells, but not in adult cells.
source: We found that BCR cross-linking increased the phosphorylation of PKC in neonatal CD19+CD43- cells, but not in adult cells (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: FAK was constitutively phosphorylated at Tyr397 in neonatal cells and this phosphorylation increased further after stimulation.
source: FAK was constitutively phosphorylated at Tyr397 in neonatal cells and this phosphorylation increased further after stimulation, whereas BCR cross-linking triggered a comparable increase in phosphorylation at Tyr567 in adults and neonates (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the FAK catalytic activity did not lead to the unique STAT5 phosphorylation in neonates.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: BCR cross-linking triggered a comparable increase in FAK phosphorylation at Tyr567 in adults and neonates.
source: FAK was constitutively phosphorylated at Tyr397 in neonatal cells and this phosphorylation increased further after stimulation, whereas BCR cross-linking triggered a comparable increase in phosphorylation at Tyr567 in adults and neonates (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the FAK catalytic activity did not lead to the unique STAT5 phosphorylation in neonates.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The FAK catalytic activity did not lead to the unique STAT5 phosphorylation in neonates.
source: FAK was constitutively phosphorylated at Tyr397 in neonatal cells and this phosphorylation increased further after stimulation, whereas BCR cross-linking triggered a comparable increase in phosphorylation at Tyr567 in adults and neonates (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the FAK catalytic activity did not lead to the unique STAT5 phosphorylation in neonates.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparable Tyr567 phosphorylation in adults and neonates.

claim: Both the PKC inhibitor staurosporine and the FAK inhibitor 14 (F-14) inhibited neonatal BCR-induced STAT5 phosphorylation.
source: Confirming their upstream role in controlling STAT5 activation, both the PKC inhibitor staurosporine and the FAK inhibitor 14 (F-14) inhibited neonatal BCR-induced STAT5 phosphorylation (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Il6 gene expression in response to neonatal BCR engagement was impeded by PKC inhibitor, FAK inhibitor, and STAT5 inhibitor.
source: Moreover, Il6 gene expression in response to neonatal BCR engagement was impeded by these inhibitors as well as the STAT5 inhibitor (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The Rac1 inhibitor, NSC23766 inhibited STAT5 phosphorylation following BCR cross-linking.
source: Also, the Rac1 inhibitor, NSC23766 inhibited STAT5 phosphorylation (Figure 6D) and Il6 gene expression (Figure 6E) following BCR cross-linking.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The Rac1 inhibitor, NSC23766 inhibited Il6 gene expression following BCR cross-linking.
source: Also, the Rac1 inhibitor, NSC23766 inhibited STAT5 phosphorylation (Figure 6D) and Il6 gene expression (Figure 6E) following BCR cross-linking.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: PKC was phosphorylated in both adult and neonatal CD19+CD43- cells after PMA stimulation.
source: As expected, PKC was phosphorylated in both adult and neonatal CD19+CD43- cells after PMA stimulation (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: PMA induced the phosphorylation of p65 and IκBα in both neonatal and adult CD19+CD43- cells.
source: Also, PMA induced the phosphorylation of p65 and IκBα in both neonatal and adult CD19+CD43- cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Only neonatal B cells manifested STAT5 phosphorylation in response to PMA.
source: However, only neonatal B cells manifested STAT5 phosphorylation in response to PMA (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Spleen tyrosine kinase (Syk) and Btk control BCR-induced STAT5 phosphorylation.
source: Finally, by using specific inhibitors, we found that spleen tyrosine kinase (Syk) and Btk control BCR-induced STAT5 phosphorylation (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: BCR cross-linking did not increase CD19+CD43+IL-10+ population in both wild-type and IL-6 KO cells.
source: We found that the BCR cross-linking did not increase CD19+CD43+IL-10+ population in both wild-type and IL-6 KO cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: BCR-induced IL-6 does not promote the expression of IL-10 by B-1 population.
source: Thus, BCR-induced IL-6 does not promote the expression of IL-10 by B-1 population.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: IL-10 derived from Bregs has a major role in inhibiting inflammatory cytokine production by monocytes.
source: IL-10 derived from Bregs has a major role in inhibiting inflammatory cytokine production by monocytes (Iwata et al., 2011; Ray et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Iwata et al., 2011 and Ray et al., 2012.

claim: Neonatal B cells have been shown to restrict Th1 responses in vivo and ex vivo by suppressing myeloid cell functions in an IL-10-dependent manner.
source: Neonatal B cells have been shown to restrict Th1 responses in vivo and ex vivo by suppressing myeloid cell functions in an IL-10-dependent manner (Zhang et al., 2007; Sun et al., 2005; Walker and Goldstein, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2007; Sun et al., 2005; and Walker and Goldstein, 2007.

claim: CM from WT neonatal CD19+CD43- cells contained the highest amount of IL-10.
source: We confirmed that CM from WT neonatal CD19+CD43- cells contained the highest amount of IL-10 (Figure 7A), whereas all three CMs contained low amount of TNF-α (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: All three CMs (adult, WT neonatal, and IL-6 KO neonatal) contained low amount of TNF-α.
source: We confirmed that CM from WT neonatal CD19+CD43- cells contained the highest amount of IL-10 (Figure 7A), whereas all three CMs contained low amount of TNF-α (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Unstimulated cell-CMs from all three groups failed to induce TNF-α production when incubated with macrophages.
source: When incubated with macrophages, unstimulated cell-CMs from all three groups failed to induce TNF-α production (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: In the presence of control antibody (Rat IgG1), CMs from anti-IgM-stimulated adult and IL-6 KO neonatal cells elicited significant and comparable increases in TNFα production.
source: In the presence of control antibody (Rat IgG1), CMs from anti-IgM-stimulated adult and IL-6 KO neonatal cells elicited significant and comparable increases in TNFα production (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: CM from anti-IgM-stimulated wild-type neonatal cells triggered a blunted TNF-α production from macrophages.
source: In sharp contrast, CM from anti-IgM-stimulated wild-type neonatal cells triggered a blunted TNF-α production from macrophages.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: IL-10R antibodies significantly increased the TNF-α production from macrophages incubated with CM from wild-type neonatal CD19+CD43- cells and restored its concentration to macrophages incubated with neonatal IL-6 KO CM.
source: Suggesting a suppressive role for the elevated IL-10 levels in the CM from wild-type neonatal CD19+CD43- cells, IL-10R antibodies significantly increased the TNF-α production and restored its concentration to macrophages incubated with neonatal IL-6 KO CM.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Addition of anti-IL-10R antibodies did not significantly alter the TNF-α production in macrophages incubated with adult and IL-6 KO CMs.
source: Since adult and IL-6 KO CM contained low IL-10 levels, addition of anti-IL-10R antibodies did not significantly alter the TNF-α production in macrophages incubated with these CMs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The propensity of neonatal splenic B cells to produce IL-10 with suppressive properties is well established.
source: The propensity of neonatal splenic B cells to produce IL-10 with suppressive properties is well established (Burdin et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Burdin et al., 1997.

claim: The increased IL-10 production by neonatal splenic B cells is primarily attributed to the B-1 cells, which constitute approximately 30% of B cells in neonatal spleen compared to less than 5% in adult spleen.
source: The increased IL-10 production by neonatal splenic B cells is primarily attributed to the B-1 cells, which constitute approximately 30% of B cells in neonatal spleen compared to less than 5% in adult spleen (Hayakawa et al., 1983).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hayakawa et al., 1983.

claim: The IL-10-dependent suppression of inflammation by B10 cells is well documented in adult mouse autoimmune, allergy and infection models.
source: The IL-10-dependent suppression of inflammation by B10 cells is well documented in adult mouse autoimmune, allergy and infection models (Yanaba et al., 2008; Amu et al., 2010; Jeong et al., 2012; Horikawa et al., 2013; Jeong et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yanaba et al., 2008; Amu et al., 2010; Jeong et al., 2012; Horikawa et al., 2013; and Jeong et al., 2016.

claim: BCR-stimulation is not sufficient to induce the production of IL-10 from adult B10 cells.
source: Despite the well-established requirement for antigen-mediated BCR signaling in B10 cell development, BCR-stimulation is not sufficient to induce the production of IL-10 from adult B10 cells (Yanaba et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yanaba et al., 2009.

claim: Anti-IgM stimulation inhibits IL-10 production from LPS- and CD40L-stimulated B10 cells.
source: In fact, not only anti-IgM stimulation does not induce the secretion of IL-10 from adult B10 cells, but it also inhibits IL-10 production from LPS- and CD40L-stimulated B10 cells (Yanaba et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yanaba et al., 2009.

claim: B-1 cells secrete IL-10 spontaneously and the secretion of IL-10 is further increased following BCR-stimulation.
source: In contrast to CD19+CD43- B cells, B-1 cells secrete IL-10 spontaneously and the secretion of IL-10 is further increased following BCR-stimulation (Alhakeem et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Alhakeem et al., 2015.

claim: The BCR-mediated IL-10 production from B-1 cells depends on p38 MAPK activity.
source: The BCR-mediated IL-10 production from B-1 cells depends on p38 MAPK activity (Alhakeem et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Alhakeem et al., 2015.

claim: Neonatal SH2 binding site (Tyr397) on FAK was constitutively phosphorylated.
source: We also demonstrated that neonatal SH2 binding site (Tyr397) on FAK was constitutively phosphorylated, and this phosphorylation was required for STAT5 phosphorylation because the FAK inhibitor, F-14 which inhibits phosphorylation at Tyr397 effectively blocked BCR-induced STAT5 phosphorylation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and 6B.

claim: Phosphorylation of FAK at Tyr397 was required for STAT5 phosphorylation.
source: We also demonstrated that neonatal SH2 binding site (Tyr397) on FAK was constitutively phosphorylated, and this phosphorylation was required for STAT5 phosphorylation because the FAK inhibitor, F-14 which inhibits phosphorylation at Tyr397 effectively blocked BCR-induced STAT5 phosphorylation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: FAK scaffold functions were essential to mediate BCR signaling to STAT5 in neonatal B cells.
source: These results indicated that FAK scaffold functions were essential to mediate BCR signaling to STAT5 in neonatal B cells as has been shown for FLT3 receptor signaling in oncogenic cells (Chatterjee et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and a citation to Chatterjee et al., 2014.

claim: Rac1 has been shown to have a role in STAT5 activation in several types of cells.
source: A member of Rho family of GTPases, Rac1 has been shown to have a role in STAT5 activation in several types of cells (Benitah et al., 2003; Kawashima et al., 2006) and Rac1 functions as a downstream effector of FAK (Chatterjee et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Benitah et al., 2003 and Kawashima et al., 2006.

claim: Rac1 functions as a downstream effector of FAK.

evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chatterjee et al., 2014.

claim: Induction of IL-10 secretion from Breg cells by IL-6 has been shown previously in adult mice.
source: Induction of IL-10 secretion from Breg cells by IL-6 has been shown previously by Rosser and colleagues in adult mice (Rosser et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rosser et al., 2014.

claim: IL-6, as well as IL-1β, produced by macrophages in response to microbiota mediated stimuli act on splenic and lymph node Breg cells to produce IL-10.
source: However, in this study the authors have discovered that IL-6, as well as IL-1β, produced by macrophages in response to microbiota mediated stimuli act on splenic and lymph node Breg cells to produce IL-10.
evidence: This is a reference to findings by Rosser et al., 2014.

claim: Microbiota-derived IL-6 and IL-1β required simultaneous CD40 signaling to induce IL-10 production from adult Breg cells.
source: An important distinction between our findings in neonatal CD19+CD43- B cells and those of Rosser and colleagues in adult Breg cells is that whereas microbiota-derived IL-6 and IL-1β required simultaneous CD40 signaling to induce IL-10 production from adult Breg cells, IL-6 alone was able to stimulate the production of IL-10 from neonatal CD19+CD43- B cells.
evidence: This is a reference to findings by Rosser et al., 2014.

claim: IL-6 alone was able to stimulate the production of IL-10 from neonatal CD19+CD43- B cells.
source: An important distinction between our findings in neonatal CD19+CD43- B cells and those of Rosser and colleagues in adult Breg cells is that whereas microbiota-derived IL-6 and IL-1β required simultaneous CD40 signaling to induce IL-10 production from adult Breg cells, IL-6 alone was able to stimulate the production of IL-10 from neonatal CD19+CD43- B cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: The independence of neonatal CD19+CD43- B cells from CD40 signaling in IL-6-induced IL-10 secretion has in vivo relevance because neonatal B cells do not get activated through CD40 due to weak CD40L expression in neonatal T cells.
source: The independence of neonatal CD19+CD43- B cells from CD40 signaling in IL-6-induced IL-10 secretion has in vivo relevance because neonatal B cells do not get activated through CD40 due to weak CD40L expression in neonatal T cells (Durandy et al., 1995; Fuleihan et al., 1994).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings and citations to Durandy et al., 1995 and Fuleihan et al., 1994.

claim: Recombinant IL-6 was not able to induce IL-10 production from adult CD19+CD43- B cells.
source: As was observed by Rosser and colleagues (Rosser et al., 2014), we also found that recombinant IL-6 was not able to induce IL-10 production from adult CD19+CD43- B cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and a citation to Rosser et al., 2014.

claim: The beneficial effect of IL-6 in the generation of adult T follicular helper (Tfh) cells is well recognized.
source: The beneficial effect of IL-6 in the generation of adult T follicular helper (Tfh) cells, which help activate germinal center B cells to differentiate into plasma cells and memory B cells in response to immunization and infection is well recognized (Korn and Hiltensperger, 2021; Papillion et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Korn and Hiltensperger, 2021 and Papillion et al., 2019.

claim: In contrast to adults, IL-6 suppresses vaccine response in neonatal mice by inhibiting Tfh generation and expanding the suppressive T follicular regulatory helper (Tfr) cells.
source: We have previously shown that, in contrast to adults, IL-6 suppresses vaccine response in neonatal mice by inhibiting Tfh generation and expanding the suppressive T follicular regulatory helper (Tfr) cells (Yang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yang et al., 2018.
